speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is obviously a sizeable gap between how safe Singaporeans feel online and offline.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, most of us remain connected online throughout the day.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Online services have become the key conduits through which we communicate and consume content.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill we are debating today is not the first law introduced to secure our online space.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Government has, over the years, introduced targeted laws to deal with specific types of harmful online content and behaviour, including: (a) Falsehoods, which are dealt with under the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act, or POFMA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (b) Foreign interference, which is addressed under the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act, or FICA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (c) Online harassment, such as cyberbullying, which is dealt with under the Protection from Harassment Act, or POHA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: POHA was also recently updated in 2019 to cover doxxing.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our laws have served to protect many Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: POFMA was integral to Singapore's response to COVID-19, allowing the Government to address the deluge of misinformation which made COVID-19 not just a pandemic, but an "info-demic".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Recently, The Straits Times reported a record high number of protection orders filed and granted in 2021 under POHA, more than double the number in previous years.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Lawyers attributed the spike in applications to media attention on the issue of harassment.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The application process has also been enhanced with the opening of the Protection from Harassment Court.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, there are still gaps that need to be addressed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One growing concern is content encouraging suicide and self-harm.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Just two months ago, an investigation in the United Kingdom (UK) concluded that 14-year-old Molly Russell took her own life after being exposed to thousands of self-harm and suicide related posts in the months leading up to her death.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many of these posts portrayed suicide as an inevitable consequence of depression.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There have also been reports of users' accidental deaths while attempting to mimic videos of impossible physical stunts.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unknown to some victims, these reckless acts and dangerous challenges had been heavily edited.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our children, who may lack the capacity or maturity to deal with certain types of content are particularly vulnerable when exposed to inappropriate content and unwanted social interaction online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In June this year, MCI conducted a study which asked respondents what online content they felt children needed to be most protected from.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The top three were sexual content, cyberbullying and violent content.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In a dialogue with youths held by MCI and the National Youth Council last year, participants indicated that the top three online harms they and their peers faced included being insulted online, impersonated by someone else and receiving unwanted contact from another person.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If such harmful content existed only on websites, the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) would be able to deal with them under the existing Broadcasting Act.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But today, users are much more likely to consume content from the feeds of social media services, where such harmful content can be pushed via algorithms, and spread quickly through our social connections.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Just two weeks ago, Meta announced that Facebook recorded nearly 2 billion daily users, while Instagram recorded 2 billion active monthly users.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: TikTok has been downloaded over 3.5 billion times worldwide since its launch, while YouTube recorded 30 billion daily views on "YouTube Shorts".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As the Internet evolves, so must our laws.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the book "Tools and Weapons" co-authored by Microsoft's President Brad Smith and Carol Ann Browne, the backwardness of some cybersecurity measures was likened to "digging trenches to defend against missiles".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To ensure that Singapore users of these services and platforms can be kept safe, we must be able to take appropriate action on these entities, as long as they provide content accessible by Singapore users.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are not alone in thinking this way.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is a growing consensus that rules must be put in place to prevent harms in the online world, just as in the physical world.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Calls for online services to take greater responsibility in ensuring safety on their platforms have also led to jurisdictions such as the UK, the European Union (EU), Germany and Australia to introduce or propose new online safety laws.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Respondents expressed the desire for safety features to manage their exposure to certain types of content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Similarly, MCI's June 2022 study, found that nine in 10 respondents felt that such measures would protect users from harmful online content to at least a moderate extent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Parents, in particular, were concerned over viral social media content which featured dangerous pranks and challenges, harmful advertising, cyberbullying and explicit sexual content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some suggested keeping younger users in mind when developing safety features, including tailoring content moderation thresholds and ensuring young users can easily report inappropriate content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In a separate poll conducted earlier this year by the Sunlight Alliance for Action, Singaporeans ranked reporting systems and laws to tackle online harms as the top two measures that would facilitate help-seeking.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will now explain our approach to enhancing online safety for Singapore users and Members will find that there are similarities to the practices elsewhere, examples of which I have circulated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The first is to tackle the problems in an accretive manner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Rather than take a "Big Bang" approach which some countries are attempting and have an all-encompassing law, let us design our laws in a considered and calibrated manner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, as far as possible, be outcome driven instead of being overly prescriptive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In today's context, we are dealing with a vast volume of user-generated content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Rather than chasing individual pieces of content, we must ensure that systems and processes to regulate the content are put in place and maintained by the platforms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead of prescribing how these systems and processes are set up, we should specify the outcomes they ought to achieve.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The third, and perhaps, most important of all, is to recognise that laws are not a silver bullet.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government will need to work with partners, including our citizens, to tackle harmful content and enhance the safety of users online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today's online content service providers are different from traditional local broadcasters and require a different regulatory approach.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, each type of service is different. "Social media services" are not the same as "over-the-top media services", which also operate differently from "game distribution services".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Bill allows us to adopt this accretive approach by building on existing laws to introduce new ones; so that over time, our foundations for digital safety become stronger.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The regulations will only apply to specified types of "online communication service", which are listed in a Schedule under the Broadcasting Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For now, we will only specify one type of OCS in the Schedule and that is "social media services".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under the Bill, a social media service is defined as an electronic service, whose sole or primary purpose is to enable online interaction or linking between two or more users, including enabling users to share content for social purposes; and which allows users to communicate content on the service.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Why have we chosen to regulate social media services as a matter of priority?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is the highest proportion compared to other platforms, such as e-commerce sites, search engines and news sites.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Given the voluminous user-generated content in today's evolving online space, it is not efficient to regulate individual pieces of content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: IMDA will instead focus on system-wide measures which are more effective at scale.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This approach is similar to how we go about regulating fire safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Building owners, occupiers and qualified persons must adhere to the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF)'s Fire Code, which requires them to put in place systems and processes to maintain high fire safety standards, to keep their occupants safe.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Likewise, OCSs must have in place systems and processes to minimise Singapore users' exposure to, and mitigate the impact of, harmful content on their platforms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: IMDA will impose these requirements on designated OCSs via Codes of Practice.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By stating in the Codes the outcomes which regulated services must meet, IMDA aims to provide sufficient clarity on what the services must do to protect users, whilst allowing some flexibility for them to adjust their approaches.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We can also expect IMDA to update the Codes from time to time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will allow us to be agile and responsive to technologies as they evolve.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But before introducing new requirements, IMDA will consult and work collaboratively with service providers to assess the most suitable approaches to strengthening safety on their platforms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under the Bill, IMDA does not have unfettered ability to issue new Codes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The new section 45L sets out that IMDA can issue Codes for the following purposes: First, to ensure services have systems or processes in place to address harmful content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, to provide practical guidance or certainty in respect of what content should be covered.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, to set out the procedures that service providers must follow when audits are carried out.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Fourth, to require services to collaborate with approved researchers to understand systemic risks relating to the service.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Earlier, I explained that we will apply our new laws to social media services as the first type of OCS.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Let us now turn to the Code that designated social media services with significant reach or impact in Singapore must comply with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In October, IMDA issued a draft copy of the "Code of Practice for Online Safety".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This draft Code comes after an extensive study of international online safety legislation as well as proposals and engagements with major social media services in Singapore, including Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, Twitter and HardwareZone.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The social media services consulted were receptive to the proposals laid out in the draft Code and the Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They support the Government's commitment to find innovative and effective solutions to combat harmful online content and recognise the need to improve online safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The social media services must also take additional steps to minimise children's exposure to inappropriate content and provide tools allowing children or their parents to manage their safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, make available an easy-to-use mechanism for Singapore users to report harmful content and unwanted interactions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, provide transparency on the effectiveness of their measures in protecting Singapore users from harmful content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Designated social media services must provide information that reflect Singapore users' experience on their services.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will allow users to make informed decisions about how they use the service.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the Bill is passed, IMDA will further consult relevant social media services, before finalising the Code for issuance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We believe that the Code of Practice for Online Safety will reduce users' exposure to harmful online content, but it will not eliminate them completely.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Part of the reason is that these social media services tend to operate globally, drawing in users and content from around the world.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Their safety measures are not tuned to reflect an in-depth understanding of Singapore's local context or our racial and religious sensitivities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members may recall that in the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, supermarkets were purportedly running out of toilet paper.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A social media post surfaced, suggesting that people use the Bible and the Quran as toilet paper.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This post was religiously very offensive and denigrated two religions in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, it was not moderated nor removed by the platform concerned.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: IMDA had to step in to engage the platform and the platform eventually disabled access to the post.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There may also be egregious content on non-designated social media services, which are not subject to the Code of Practice for Online Safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In May last year, a poll published on a social media service sexualised local female Islamic teachers, asked users to rank them and further promoted sexual violence against them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The post went viral and the modest reach of this particular service received a sudden big boost.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It not only caused great distress to the individuals involved, but also unsettled many others in the community.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These issues are like fires that occur, even as the Fire Code has prevented most fires.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In such instances, we must have firefighters who are properly equipped to act quickly, so as to minimise, if not prevent, serious injury and damage.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: IMDA has, in fact, performed this role for some time now, working with social media services behind the scenes to deal with egregious content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Singapore's media regulator, IMDA also has significant experience in assessing content across the different media platforms and making decisions to protect the community.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under this Bill, IMDA will be better equipped to ensure Singapore users are protected from egregious content online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But IMDA will not have carte blanche to issue directions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, IMDA will not be able to issue directions in respect of private communications.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, directions can only be issued for certain categories of egregious content relating to user safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These categories will be set out in law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When dealing with content that requires the expertise of other agencies, IMDA will consult them accordingly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As an example, when assessing content pertaining to public health measures and risk, IMDA will consult the Ministry of Health (MOH) and its experts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Respondents of MCI's public consultation and engagements agreed with this view.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They wanted the Government to mandate stronger measures and social media services to do more to reduce harmful online content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, they emphasised that all of us, as users of social media services, have an individual responsibility to protect ourselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During one of our engagements, Mr Mark Joel Premraj, a parent, shared his perspective on how parents also play a key role in educating their children on inappropriate content online, including how to encourage them to flag the inappropriate content they come across.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides establishing a robust regulatory toolkit, the Government has taken active steps to nurture a well-informed and discerning public.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Efforts to educate the public include the National Library Board's S.U.R.E. programme.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It equips the public to think critically, be responsible producers and consumers of information, and stay safe and well online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, the Ministry of Education (MOE)'s refreshed Character and Citizenship Education curriculum has a stronger focus on Cyber Wellness education, where students learn to be safe, respectful and responsible users of cyberspace, and to be a positive peer influence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In support of the Digital for Life movement, launched in February last year, community partners have also spearheaded initiatives which helped over 270,000 Singaporeans enrich their lives through digital technologies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, TOUCH Community Services has partnered Meta to conduct the Digitally Ready Families programme, where low-income families learn digital life skills and cyber wellness tips.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another Digital for Life partner is "Kids PlaySafer".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Created and run by Ms Sandra Low, a mother of an 11-year-old and 9-year-old, "Kids PlaySafer" has conducted talks on digital literacy and cyber safety to help parents manage their children's digital needs.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Deputy Speaker, for many people, technology is indistinguishable from magic that greatly improves our lives and brings about greater convenience.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: However, for the parents of 14-year-old British girl, Molly Russell, social media became the dark spell that took away the life of their daughter.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Besides content about self-harm, there are many other types of harmful online content including those that promote violence, sexual abuse or enmity between races.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: That said, there is no law that can shield us totally from harmful content.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Therefore, as the Government strengthens the law, our hope is that as parents, we can encourage our children to tell us whenever they encounter problems online, so that we can support them.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Our hope is for social media platforms to innovate and come up with newer technologies to protect users, beyond just fulfilling their obligations.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: All of us also hope that while civil organisations and individuals strengthen their own awareness of such content, they can also empower vulnerable groups to counter such content.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Only then, can we move forward as one.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, let me conclude.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: When the author Arthur C Clarke published "2001: A Space Odyssey", one of the lines in the book became famous and quoted many times over.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: It says, "Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic".

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Without disturbing Parliamentary proceedings, Members can compare notes instantaneously, in fact, I saw some of you do so.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: And conduct research on the fly either directly by instructing the colleagues outside the Chamber or just looking at the QR code that I distributed.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Gone are the days where we might rush home to catch a favourite television programme.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: So much content is available online anytime, anywhere.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: But not all of this content is good.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When social media first emerged, many people saw it as an unadulterated good thing – a new frontier, separate from the real world, offering freedom of speech without ill consequences.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Indeed, the founders of many social media companies had good intentions – to connect users from around the world; to give them personal control to express what they desire and exchange ideas; to be free of oppression; to come together and do good for themselves and their societies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Years passed, and alas, we know that the reality is far from the ideal.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have seen how extremism gets propagated online, inspiring and triggering acts of terrorism in parts of the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have seen how young lives were lost to dark and depressing content, and irrational online movements such as the "Blackout challenge".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have seen how hate speeches, in the name of free speech, get disseminated and cause great divisions within society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are worrying trends that we see around the world and countries, including those that uphold democracy and free speech, are facing the same challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a society, we must respond to curb its ills and protect the vulnerable, while allowing the widest possible.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, our legislation must evolve to better protect our people from harmful online content, especially minors who are more susceptible and vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this, Singapore is not alone in passing such a legislation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Australia and Germany are some of the first few countries to have done so, and others are either doing the same, or thinking of doing the same.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Bill also represents a shift in some ways.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On the Internet, all types of information, the good and the bad, are readily accessible and can be proliferated widely almost instantaneously, thereby extending the harm it can bring onto innocent people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In instances of bullying, the Internet magnifies the effects.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And, in other instances, the widespread egregious content could mislead and cause harm to the innocent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thus, I believe that most, if not all, will agree on the importance of protecting those who are vulnerable online.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What criteria or parameters do the Ministry consider?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, I note that private messages will not be covered in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I suppose the Ministry is trying to strike a balance between offering sufficient protection whilst not being overly intrusive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, there could be instances where objectionable content gets shared through private messaging channels.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, in the context of Australia where its online safety act was passed just last year and came into effect earlier this year, private messaging is included.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could the Ministry explain the considerations made when deciding what to cover and what not to cover?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Perhaps, the Ministry could also share the lessons learnt or the observations made of other jurisdictions where similar legislation was passed before us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While I applaud the Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill for being a timely one, I would also like to know: how frequent does the Ministry intend to review the Bill?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we know, technological advancement and disruptions happen at accelerating speeds.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Along with it comes new issues and operational challenges that the Bill today may not be adequate in addressing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, with the rise of the metaverse and the increasing number of young people immersing in it, our legislation and protection mechanisms must catch up quickly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In May this year, it was reported on various news sites, such as the BBC and The Business Insider, that a researcher's avatar was sexually assaulted on a metaverse platform called the Horizon World.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The researcher from a non-profit advocacy group SumOfUs entered the particular metaverse and, within an hour, her avatar was raped in the virtual space.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As she wore her Virtual Reality (VR) equipment during that episode, her controller vibrated when the male avatar strangers touched her, resulting in a physical sensation consequential of what she was experiencing online.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It was a clear instance of how the virtual and physical world boundaries have blurred and how online happenings can cause real harm.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Apparently, that was not an isolated incident, as there were other reports of similar sexual assaults, homophobic and racial slurs, as well as gun violence on Horizon World.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I support the Bill, given the online harms that people in Singapore have been subject to on social media and on the Internet, and the growing need to protect our people, especially the young, from these harms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I have some clarifications to seek on the Bill which I hope the Minister will address before we vote on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Access to digital communication devices is not optional in this day and age, even for younger children.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, if a 10-year-old child were to take public transport on his own to and from school, his parents would want him to be able to contact them in case of an emergency or to track his location.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In most cases, this can only be done using a mobile phone or smart watch.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, it will be unwise to give that same 10-year-old unfiltered access to the Internet on his phone.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Currently, parents can install a parental control app on their child's phone.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This app will allow parents to restrict content, approve apps, set screen times and filter harmful content.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It can also locate the child using GPS.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I set this up for my son some time back.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, even with all my professional technical knowledge, it took me quite a bit of time and research to figure out which was the most suitable software to use and how to configure it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I wonder how many parents have tried to set up parental control software for their children.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For those who have not, they should be aware that their children and teens essentially have unfiltered access to the Internet and all the harms that come with it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These parents can only regulate their children's Internet access by looking over their shoulders.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a suboptimal solution, given the asymmetry of technical knowledge between most parents and their children.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most children nowadays can run rings around their parents when it comes to configuring settings on their mobile phones.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Also, for such content filtering to work for young people, age verification is needed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Code of Practice for Online Safety for Designated Social Media Services proposed by the Ministry states that social media services must have additional measures to protect children, including minimising children's exposure to inappropriate content and ensuring that their account settings are age-appropriate by default.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the Code of Practice does not prescribe how this age verification should be implemented.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, attempts at imposing age verification have previously failed in the United Kingdom's implementation of the Digital Economy Act of 2017, in part because of privacy concerns.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Online age verification providers could collect excessive personally identifiable information and process it for other purposes in violation of privacy laws.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Separately, a young user can circumvent age restrictions by declaring his age to be 18 when, in fact, he is only 12.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some Internet service providers do provide parental control tools which block harmful content before they come through the fibre.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, they require a separate subscription that entails an additional cost each month.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many parents are not even aware of this service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They will have to take the effort to log in to their broadband provider's website and subscribe to this service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will ensure that even children of less tech-savvy parents will be protected by default.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Adults who need full access to the Internet should be able to opt out of the filtering service without any charge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am glad to note that under the Code of Practice, content that may encourage young users to engage in dangerous acts will be considered harmful content and be subject to additional safeguards for young users.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Examples of these include the "Skull-breaker Challenge" where two people trick a friend standing in between them to take a vertical jump, then kick their legs from under them as they are in the air, making them fall backwards and potentially injure their head and back.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: People sometimes do not properly assess the risk associated with an activity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They may have seen others perform it without incident in a YouTube video and may be tempted to experiment themselves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, we cannot completely insulate young people from all dangerous, harmful and silly online content.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The best protection is for parents and teachers to educate their children and students of the potentially harmful content that may be accessed online and the consequences of indulging in them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Media Literacy Council could also directly push out educational materials on the platforms that young people access, like TikTok and Telegram.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This should be an ongoing process, not a one-time effort, because harmful content is constantly evolving, and new trends are always emerging.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister clarify if this fine will apply to only the company or also the individual officers within the company responsible for ensuring compliance?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given the financial might of social media companies, they might have no problem paying even a huge fine.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is so that IMDA can be kept apprised of trends in harmful online content and behaviours.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Section B of the Code of Practice requires that users of OCSs must be able to report harmful content or unwanted interactions to the platform providers through an "effective, transparent and easy to use mechanism" and social media services are expected to take action on these user reports in a "timely manner".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This leaves open lots of room for interpretation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Another potential area of harm to young people is online gaming, which can be both addictive and cause social problems.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that the Bill covers cyberbullying content that is likely to cause harassment, alarm or distress to the targeted person.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There have been cases, recently, of disgruntled ex-lovers sharing such images, which, most certainly, will cause alarm and distress to the victim.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to seek clarifications from the Minister regarding the protection of Singaporeans' democratic rights in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some respondents to the public consultation sought assurance that the proposed measures would not affect user privacy or freedom of expression.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Bill gives wide-ranging powers to IMDA to issue directions to social media companies to remove harmful content if it deems it so.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on what safeguards will be in place to ensure that such powers are not abused?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will there be channels for independent appeal or judicial review?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The UK's Online Safety Bill specifically includes protections to safeguard pluralism and ensure Internet users can continue to engage in robust debate online.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, section 29 of the latest draft of the UK's Online Safety Bill requires content providers to "have regard to the importance of protecting the rights of users and interested persons to freedom of expression within the law", when deciding on safety measures and policies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Section 15 of the UK Bill also requires social media services to put in place clear policies to protect "content of democratic importance", such as user-submitted comments supporting or opposing particular political parties or policies, and to enforce this consistently across all content moderation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The UK Bill also requires that platforms must not discriminate against different political viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The UK's draft legislation has also been designed to safeguard access to journalistic content.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: News publishers' content will be exempted from social media platforms' new online safety regulations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Because of this, social media platforms will not be incentivised to remove news publishers' content, as a result of a fear of sanction from the regulator.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are there such provisions in Singapore's Online Safety Bill?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If not, will the Government study the Online Safety Bills of other countries, including the UK and Australia, and include democratic protections in the Code of Practice and subsidiary legislation?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will Singapore have the equivalent of an eSafety Commissioner like Australia does?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Who will this eSafety Commissioner be, and will he or she be empowered to make directions independent of the Government?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Australia's Online Safety Act itself was controversial in part because of the huge amount of discretion and power it puts in the hands of the Minister for Communications and the eSafety Commissioner to determine what are community expectations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How will Singapore's Bill safeguard democratic freedoms while protecting the young from online harms?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that some electronic services are excluded from this Bill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Examples of these are SMS and MMS services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I confirm with the Minister that other private messaging platforms like WhatsApp, Telegram and Signal are also excluded from this Bill?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For the avoidance of doubt, I am not advocating for these services to be included in this Bill, as they are primarily used for private communication between individuals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Much of the communication is end-to-end encrypted, which means even the platforms do not have access to the data exchanged by their users.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would have strong privacy concerns if this encryption were to be broken for the sake of enhancing online safety.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It has a deep impact on how we learn, how we do business and how we interact with one another.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, because of the cloak of anonymity, the online world rears its ugly head through online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Maintaining safety online is not just the responsibility of the individual or the Government but all stakeholders involved.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, many felt that stricter enforcement of relevant laws can be effective to combat or reduce online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many also felt that technology companies and platforms must lead the way in tackling this issue, alongside the Government and us fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is, thus, timely that we have this Bill to further help us safeguard Singaporeans against online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last week, my firm organised its annual thought leadership platform, the Dentons Rodyk Dialogue 2022, themed "Building a Safe and Inclusive Digital World Together: Vision and Transformation".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During the keynote speech, Minister Josephine Teo explained Singapore's approach in regulation towards digital safety and inclusion by ensuring what she described as the "3As".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, agglomerate – pulling in partners and groups in our collective endeavour.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Third, agile – being able to adapt through different emerging technology or disruptions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To borrow from bonds credit rating parlance, that to me, is a triple-A rated approach – sound and sensible.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In dealing with online harms, it is important to take a calibrated and multi-stakeholder approach while keeping a close eye on emerging technologies, such as Web 3.0 and the metaverse.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although Bill is focused on platform and service providers, there is also a need to focus on the users, particularly, the victims of online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The bulk of the cases they face are time-sensitive given the viral nature of the harmful online content, but most importantly, they are emotionally draining and usually, it is time- and cost-consuming for victims to seek redress.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Following this initiative, together with other People's Action Party (PAP) Members of Parliament, like Ms Hany Soh and Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin, we spearheaded the formation of resource toolkit to combat online harms at the PAP Women's Wing International Women's Day celebration in March this year.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And in September this year, with the help of pro bono lawyers, social workers and counsellors, we ran a workshop for close to 70 activists across various PAP branches on the practical walkthrough of the resource toolkit.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is to support residents during Meet-the-People sessions or any of our other activities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, raising awareness and empowerment is a continuing endeavour.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   In June 2021, I started an initiative called Defence Guild SG.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This was in the wake of a harassment incident towards 17 local religious teachers, who became victims of a lewd online survey.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This issue raised awareness among many within our community about the threat of online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over 20 lawyers from different races and religions, comprising of veteran and young lawyers from the Lawyers@M³ network, joined forces to provide legal advice to victims of online harassment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most of the cases they dealt with are sensitive in nature and many within our community are unaware of the type of help available as well as their own rights.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): I now move away from the individual and on to the service providers, the focus of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have several clarifications: firstly, I would like to clarify on the definitions used in the Bill; the second set of clarifications relate to the mechanism of the takedown and defence available; and lastly, I have some clarifications and suggestions in relation to the Code of Practice proposed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In determining whether a broadcasting service is private or domestic, the new section 2(3) of the Broadcasting Act gave regard to certain factors, and I will touch on two of them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The clause itself does not state, for guidance, the actual number as a threshold.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, may I ask what would the threshold be?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Should it be a percentage of entire users of the service who are in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some clarity in this regard would be helpful.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would content on accounts which are accessible through friends or restricted followers, be considered "private or domestic nature"?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, in respect of the new clause 45D which sets out the definition of "egregious content", I have a few questions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, what is meant by content that "advocates or instructs"?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry consider content to be harmful by looking objectively at its impact on our society, even though the content itself may not provide a clear set of instructions or advocate a certain position?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, on resources, may I ask who will be the enforcement agency for this?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And would there be a dedicated team to regulate such behaviour?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And if so, how are we sufficiently resourced for this?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, in Australia, the Department of Home Affairs has a dedicated team to find content on social media sites that promote hate, incite violence, or points to terrorist propaganda.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is a resource-intensive endeavour, and if we rely on self-reporting by individuals or self-regulation by providers, there may be many instances of online harms that fall through the crack.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thirdly, I note that certain categories of harms are expressly stated in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the takedown or disabling order under clause 45H and the blocking order under clause 45I.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is also a defence available to service providers in not complying with the order, if it was not reasonably practicable to do more than what was in fact done, or if there was no better practicable means than what was in fact used.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, may I ask what is meant by "reasonably practicable"?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the costs or expenses involved in complying with such order be a relevant factor?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, what about actual or consequential loss that the party may suffer when complying with such duty?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would suggest that such costs, expenses and losses are not relevant factors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because economic losses or ramifications should not be placed on equal importance footing with online harms that have debilitating and irreversible effects on our society and individuals.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, I would welcome Minister's clarifications in this regard.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, in relation to the immunity given to service providers against criminal or civil liability when complying with the orders – under clause 45J.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would this apply to civil liability brought by parties from outside the jurisdiction as well?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand and fully appreciate that our laws may not have extraterritorial effect in this respect.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am fully aware that the current Bill, as proposed, was done after extensive consultation with service providers and platforms and that they are supportive of such proposals.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Other jurisdictions have also passed similar legislation to safeguard against online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps the Ministry can also explore reciprocal immunity provisions with other like-minded jurisdictions in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would help harmonise and set an international standard for compliance of cross-border directions in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My next clarification is in relation to clause 45H(1)(d) on the period of takedown notice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This reflects the imminent risk of such online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If there is a standard fixed period by legislation, it will lead to a reasonable expectation or standard within the industry for compliance and sufficient company internal compliance processes can be put in place to meet with such expectations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, may I clarify what is meant by clause 45H(2)(b), that a requirement "must not require the doing of anything with respect to the provision of an online communication service to the whole or part of any area in Singapore"?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps, can Minister provide an example for this?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that the a Code of Practice can be revised or amended pursuant to a process to be followed, which allows for future flexibility and adaptability.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My question is, given the fluidity and dynamic nature of our digital ecosystem, would the Code be able to keep up with the changes brought upon by the rapid changes in technology?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I note that there is a process before a change in Code can be made, as envisaged at clause 45L.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps, if I may suggest the formation of a council to formulate and update the Code regularly to keep up with technology trends?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such Council can comprise of service providers, regulators, important law enforcement or community stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding the above clarifications, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I support the thrust of the Bill and stand in agreement with the arguments made by my Parliamentary colleague, Aljunied Member of Parliament, Mr Gerald Giam.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In particular, I strongly support Mr Giam's call on the Government to provide clear and unequivocal assurances that this law will not be used to curtail the exercise of legitimate free speech that touches on the public acts of public figures and that is not of a vicious and personal nature.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government can provide such assurances during the Parliamentary debate, to be recorded in the Hansard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I address these two topics, let me make some general suggestions and clarifications on the approach taken in this Bill, where more clarity is, perhaps, needed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In addition to such measures and perhaps embedded in the Codes of Practice, I wonder if there could be a system where users of OCSs can first report content on the platform that is egregious and/or seriously harassing, to the OCS itself.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If the OCS fails to take action within a stipulated time frame, say seven days, then there could be a mechanism whereby the complainant can raise this issue to the IMDA and ask the IMDA to issue the appropriate directions in relation to such content.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One of its features is that a person may make a complaint to eSafety about cyberbullying material that targets an Australian child and this acts as a safety net, because they must have first reported the material to the relevant online service provider before taking the step.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In addition, if the OCS fails to investigate or take action about that content reported by a user within the stipulated time frame, there could be penalties for the OCS.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While there are already reporting platforms or tools on most, if not all, of the OCSs, such a requirement embedded in a Code of Practice would create some legal pressure on the OCS to further investigate and act on user notifications or reports of egregious content in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While this section does contain some specific definitions of egregious content, there could be other types of egregious content where more specificity would be welcome, as my colleague Mr Giam and other Members alluded to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But at paragraph 4 of the First Reading speech, the June 2022 survey by MCI found that, "Sexual content, cyberbullying and violent content were the top three types of content that respondents felt the young needed to be protected from most".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And I was actually not referring to the speech, but to the statement from MCI.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It would seem that the proposed Bill might not address the first two concerns in a sufficiently specific manner.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In Canada, there is an offence of sharing intimate images without consent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I hope the subsidiary legislation can be more specific about these two types of egregious content.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Madam, I note that at paragraph 8 of the Ministry's statement. it is stated that "The Codes of Practice may require Regulated Online Communication Services (ROCS) providers to put in place measures on their services to mitigate the risks of danger to Singapore users from exposure to harmful content and provide accountability to their users on such measures." I would like to ask the Government how this accountability will come about.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Will the Government commit to public consultations when new Codes of Practice are issued?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is hinted at in section 45L(2), but it is not a requirement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I hope that, given the evolving nature of online harms, as well as the need to balance privacy and free speech concerns, that a proper consultation process will be the norm in future before new Codes of Practice are issued.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Madam, part 9(d) of the same statement refers to how ROCS providers should collaborate or cooperate with the conduct of research studies by experts approved by IMDA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such research would allow IMDA to understand the nature and level of the systemic risks in the ROCS, and the evolution and severity of such risks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is a very positive move for MCI to formally refer to the use of research in this manner, since this area of online harms is a rapidly evolving space and since more research needs to be done on the effects of certain online activities, particularly on children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is not a small number by any means.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is traumatic for the child and can leave lasting psychological scars.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But it is also hard on the parents, arousing feelings of concern, frustrations and yet, helplessness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Because sometimes, the parents feels that they cannot address the problem with a sledgehammer, by coming down hard on the bullies, who are themselves children and may not fully understand what they are doing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think the Minister had referred to this example as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Her classmate's mother had created a fake MySpace account, pretending to be a teenage boy, Josh. "Josh" messaged Megan on AOL Instant Messenger (AIM) saying something very hurtful.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am not advocating for law enforcement agencies to police private conversations in a way that compromises privacy, could itself be subject to executive over-reach and could corrode our children's capacity to spontaneously interact with one another as well as learn social lessons thereby.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would suggest that for now, the problem can be addressed through education and would like to call on MOE and the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to explore this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are helplines for young victims of bullying, including cyberbullying, such as Tinkle Friend by the Singapore Children's Society, which does good work and deserves support from all of us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am also aware that cyberbullying is addressed in the current curriculum relating to cyber wellness in schools.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would urge the Government to conduct further research into this area and study innovative programmes that have worked around the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But does this translate to bystanders pushing back when bullying actually happens online?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And perhaps video clips and other communications material can be rolled out to a mass audience featuring such anti-bullying ambassadors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Next, Madam, let me move onto the subject of loot boxes and other gambling-like elements in electronic games.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The most recent was in 2019 which elicited the reply that the Remote Gambling Act (RGA) would apply to loot boxes, only if the loot thus obtained could potentially be converted into real world money.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: To quote from that 2019 reply, "Given the randomness of the prizes in loot boxes, they are a game of chance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: However, whether the loot boxes are considered a form of gambling under the RGA, depends on whether there are in-game facilities that allow players to convert game credits or any in-game items, for example, weapons and skills, to real-world money or merchandises." I also spoke about this subject in the 2020 MHA Committee of Supply (COS) debate, pointing out that loot boxes, a consumable virtual item used to redeem a randomised selection of further virtual items, are increasingly seen, in some quarters, as a form of gambling.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I highlighted that from a study by academics at the University of York, there is some evidence linking loot boxes to problem gambling.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Its mental health director Claire Murdoch warned that these were in danger of "setting kids up for addiction." Since my 2020 speech in this House, fresh research has strengthened the evidence of a causative link between loot boxes and problem gambling.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Twelve out of 13 studies on the topic have established 'unambiguous' connections to problem gambling behaviour…The big spenders – the crucial 5% for the industry – can spend more than £70 or £100 a month on the boxes", the report said.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: A report from the Norwegian Consumer Council from May 2022 suggests that some of these in-game gambling-like elements "contribute to a sense of anticipation and reward and are presumably designed to trigger dopamine releases that keep the player opening packs." Madam, my concern is that, aside from young children spending money in something that is potentially of little benefit, there is the risk that our young children playing these games, or perhaps a significant minority of them craving that dopamine hit, could experience changes in their brain chemistry that would render them more susceptible to problem gambling as adults.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The studies I cited shows that there is some evidence to support this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I hope that stronger action will be taken against such elements in games, beyond just a dollar cap.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: To be sure, electronic games can nurture positive traits, such as strategic thinking, information processing and mental agility.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But the elements in some games which suggest that players can pay to play, but with randomised results, could well result in mental habituation and attraction towards gambling later in life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If the Government will not ban such elements outright, as I hope it will, I hope, at the very least, that it would mandate warning labels on games that would draw parents' attention to the potential links to problem gambling.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That would serve as a nudge to game developers to remove such elements from their games.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I hope that such measures can be incorporated into the subsidiary legislation for this Bill or to another Act.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Users need not disclose their true identities and profiles.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rogues, under this dark cover, send out harmful content.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The proposals to require OCSs with significant reach to comply with the new Code of Practice will go some way to reduce Singapore users' exposure to such materials.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have a clarification regarding the term "Singapore users".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does this apply to all users who register, or have accounts set up in Singapore, or base their Internet Protocol (IP) addresses in Singapore at the point of registration?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, do the restrictions apply at point of access subsequently, namely their IP addresses?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another query is about Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) which are increasingly popular with users.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With VPNs, how would the Ministry ensure that Singapore users would not be exposed to harmful content?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, would the Ministry elaborate on the definition of harmful content within the Singapore context and legal perspective?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In dealing with OCSs with global reach, there may be some differences between desirable and undesirable, Eastern and Western values.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even what most of us agree on protecting children from, such as violence, cyberbullying and sexual content, have grey areas, especially for teenagers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry can share its perspective on this.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Twitter staff's ability to prevent misinformation and hate messages has been greatly reduced.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In such situations, how would the Ministry ensure that we are able to enforce the controls on such platforms?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the boundarylessness of social media has increased our access to information, eased communications with friends and family, and facilitated freedom of expression, it has also, inadvertently, exposed us to potentially undesirable content.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe the Minister had referenced these in her speech yesterday.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, I believe more can be done to help Singaporeans, especially our children and youths, navigate the World Wide Web where nefarious contents might lurk and negatively impact them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am thus heartened to know that this Bill seeks to introduce new safeguards into the Broadcasting Act (1994) by regulating online communication services (OCS), including social media services.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, algorithms on social media platforms are designed to maximise users’ engagement by creating as many ways users can interact with them as possible and by appealing to what interests their users the most.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is good that we are now considering how we can hold OCS more accountable and responsible for the type of content they carry, to limit the negative impact of egregious online content on our community and society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Cambridge Dictionary defines “egregious” as “extremely bad in a way that is very noticeable.” Using this definition, I believe that some content on OCS would clearly be regarded as egregious, for example, materials that encourage and instruct one on how to commit suicide, supporting and promoting communal violence, videos that preach intolerance, extremism, terrorism and so on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, not all content on OCS is so clear-cut.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, consider the now infamous “Blackout Challenge” that encourages participants to choke themselves until they pass out has actually claimed the lives of several youths and young children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the Government’s stand on such questionable social media trends?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would be interested to know how online materials that might not be so overtly and blatantly harmful would be regarded if there is the potential for them to be harmful.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some viral Internet challenges posted on OCS, while not overtly life-threatening at first glance, might have the potential to lead to significant public nuisances, injuries and possibly the loss of life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I must admit, Mr Deputy Speaker, as a parent of a 14- and 11-year-old, I would always want to err on the side of caution, but I also realise if we take that to the extreme, then we run the risk of anything with the slightest level of danger being banned.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be good to have some clarity on this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we debate on what is egregious content, I would like to ask what the Government's stand would be with regard to egregious behaviour.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the aim is to keep the online space safe, as indicated in the title of the Bill, then behaviour that is egregious should also be dealt with.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By this, Mr Deputy Speaker, I am referring to the issue of online bullying or cyberbullying, as already referenced by other Members of the House.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Bullying, especially of young people, is something that has always been an issue, especially in schools.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, with the pervasive proliferation of the online space, the issue of cyberbullying has multiplied into something that we cannot take lightly.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For children and youths, cyberbullying can be intense, overwhelming, psychologically harmful and can result in mental health issues, poor academic performance, school avoidance and even suicide ideation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While our counsellors and psychologists no doubt continue to work with the victims of cyberbullying and they are doing great work, I am sure, can we and should we expect the OCS to do more in this area?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Government can introduce measures to protect individuals from harmful content, individuals need to also exercise self- and social responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be impractical and impossible for the Government to monitor all contents on OCS.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A large part of social monitoring would have to be done by end-users themselves.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When end-users come across questionable content, would there be a dedicated Government-administered portal for them to provide feedback to?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or would end-users be expected to file reports with the respective OCS?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, it is also unrealistic to ban anything that seems remotely harmful or dangerous as that would over “nannify” the online space.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, I accept that what is deemed harmful and dangerous is, in itself, subjective.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe this was from the documentary, "The Social Dilemma", which, if you have not seen it on Netflix, I would recommend all Members of the House to watch as a very sobering insight into how social media works.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Jaron Lainer says: “We’ve created a world in which online connection has become primary, especially for younger generations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And yet, in that world, anytime two people connect, the only way it’s financed is through a sneaky third person who’s paying to manipulate those two people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, we’ve created an entire global generation of people who were raised within a context with the very meaning of communication, the very meaning of culture, is manipulation.” Does this manipulation lead to harmful outcomes?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My clarifications notwithstanding, I end my speech in firm support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, I would like to declare my interest as a board member of SG Her Empowerment, an Institution of Public Character that strives to empower girls and women through community engagements, partnerships and research, including on the topic of providing more holistic support to those who have faced online harms.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The proposed amendments aim to protect Singapore users from harmful online content and move beyond prescriptive statutory compliance towards public accountability.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Online platforms can enhance connectivity and access to information for users.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During COVID-19, online platforms allowed us to stay in touch and check in on each other.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But social media platforms can be all-consuming, for example, when doom-scrolling displaces other forms of interactions and feeds on one's insecurities, putting the number of friends and followers you have on display and subjecting physical appearance to visible likes and comments, sometimes, under troll anonymous accounts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For many, it is a tricky place where being yourself is simply not enough and putting yourself out there may have unwanted consequences.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These include being cyberbullied, stalked virtually and befriended by people who have fake identities.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recognising these grim realities, it is important to ensure that regulations are put in place to safeguard the online space as much as we would our physical space.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Bill sends a strong signal that the Government does not take online harms lightly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That said, I would like to highlight three specific portions where I believe there is room for the Bill to be expanded on and I will be addressing potentially sensitive issues, such as gender-based online harms and suicide, in my speech.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, the amendment tackles online harms in general, but does not specifically address the prevalence of gender-based online harms.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The gender element of online safety cannot be ignored.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Bill governs a wide range of actions by online communication services (OCS), it will not cover communications within private chat groups, such as SMS and direct messages.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Gender-based online harms take many forms and a significant proportion of these occur in private communication channels.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A number of women have shared with me that they have been on the receiving end of lewd or explicit messages.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And almost 30% of these cases took place on private message platforms, such as WhatsApp and Telegram, which is an increase in percentage from previous years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recognise that there are significant privacy concerns and logistical challenges in regulating private messaging.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, the UK's proposed Online Safety Bill came under significant fire last year for its heavy-handedness, which would have compelled online intermediaries to proactively access the content of users' private messages.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There have been cases of heavy-handed content moderation in other jurisdictions, which can be seen as an over-reach and invasion of privacy, causing individuals to lose access to their email and social media accounts, leading to much consternation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there is potential for the Bill to compel social media giants to share data, such as historical posts and messages when the user, who is a victim of image-based sexual abuse, requests it and requires evidence, for example.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, the Personal Data Protection Act already requires organisations to reveal the data they have on platform users, should the users ask for it.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In light of this, I would like to ask the Ministry what factors has it considered in deciding that the current Bill will not provide such recourse in covering private messaging channels.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Relatedly, I do appreciate that legislation exists to deal with other aspects of gender-based online harm.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, when Telegram groups have been found to distribute obscene images of women, administrators were charged under the Penal Code, including with distributing obscene material and facilitating the provision of sexual services.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Has the Government considered streamlining all online-related harms into the Online Safety Bill, rather than relying on sections in the Penal Code and Protection from Harassment Act, placing a burden on victims to show that harm has, indeed, been inflicted?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, Australia's Online Safety Act, which came into effect early this year, replaced the patchwork of online safety legislation to create a more consistent and clearer regulatory framework.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
