text: Next, more can be done to ensure that minors are protected from hyper-sexualisation or inappropriate content.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Parliament, I have spoken about the need to educate youths and parents on a safer Internet culture.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Minors are a vulnerable group who may not understand the way algorithms work to micro-target audiences with tailored messages and content who could be influenced to consume or produce content that is not age-appropriate before they have the ability to fully evaluate the harms and risks of such behaviour.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Tragically, the case of Molly Russell in the United Kingdom is a striking reminder of the very real dangers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2017, 14-year-old Molly died by suicide after viewing online content about self-harm on platforms.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Algorithms had pushed harmful materials to her accounts, some of which she had not requested.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While such devastating cases are not common, even one case is one too many and we must do all we can to prevent such occurrences from happening in Singapore, including imposing appropriate regulations and considering how we can hold the appropriate parties responsible for the content they allow on their platforms, which can also lead to other physical harms, such as eating disorders or self-injury.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But banning Internet access from our youths today is unrealistic, if not impossible.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It also fails to educate and empower them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I continue to believe that more can be done to support minors to make informed decisions about Internet content which is age-appropriate for their consumption and hope that we will continue to evaluate whether age verification is an appropriate measure to be introduced.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I note that, in the Bill, there are references to restrictions protecting children of different age groups and, indeed, the knowledge of a 13-year-old would differ from that of an 18-year-old.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would be grateful if the Ministry could share some examples of age-appropriate restrictions and how these are differentiated.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, regulating providers is only one side of the equation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Consumers of online content need to be savvy, too, and guardians need to be educated so that they are more aware of the cyber risks that their children are exposed to and feel confident to support minors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MCI has previously pointed to useful resources by the Media Literacy Council and I hope that more proactive steps are taken to directly reach out to parents and educate them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to hearing more about the Government's future efforts in this area.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, I would like to seek clarification on the definitions of egregious content.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I agree it would be appropriate for access to extremely harmful content to be disabled in Singapore – for example, when misinformation outrightly serves to sow discord between different faiths or promote violence and harms – this is only loosely described and illustrated in the Bill and consultations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This could be problematic and I also wonder whether certain forms of satirical or creative content may be affected.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When it comes to regulation in this space, there are no easy answers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recognise that in the ever-changing online space, egregious content can take many forms and, hence, it might be desirable for legislators to retain some flexibility when defining the parameters.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, in borderline cases, whose standard of egregious content will prevail?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be a committee or council to decide on these boundaries?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the Internet develops and new types of content emerge, will a deliberative body be set up to monitor and revise the definition of "egregious content"?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will such a body consult with Singaporeans to shape changes to these definitions to ensure that the standards of egregious content are widely accepted?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   Last year, a survey of an obscene nature involving 12 female relief teachers was uploaded on a social media platform.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What was even more disappointing was that over 1,000 people took part in the survey.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was a very appalling act and an affront to the dignity of women.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many women grapple with online dangers and it could cause long-term trauma.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here, I would like to ask how often the regulated OCS list will be reviewed in view of the development of social media applications and platforms, and how fast the information can be disseminated, so that any action will be taken decisively and visibly to mitigate the risk of harm to Singaporean users from exposure to harmful content and to inform their users to be responsible.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we may not be able to eradicate all harmful online content, with the introduction of this Bill and greater responsibility on the part of technology platforms, I hope we can make the Internet a safer place for everyone.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, legislation and actions taken by technology platforms alone are not enough.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Parents should also educate children about proper conduct and ethics when they are online.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, our community members, whether male or female, young or old, should not be afraid to lodge a report if they encounter any harmful content.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Deputy Speaker, Sir, the digital landscape is constantly changing and regulations will always be playing catch-up to realities on the ground.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The flexibility in the Bill demonstrates an awareness of this, allowing legislators room to respond to emerging needs and OCS providers with some leeway and timelines to address cases, depending on each circumstance's complexity.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: About 43% of them will not take action against it.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They think that it will not make a difference.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is clear that although online spaces have opened up a whole new world of information for youths, allowing them the opportunity to express themselves and connect with people globally, it has also exposed them to new forms of dangers that the previous generation has not faced, such as cyberbullying and online grooming.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I agree with these categories as they will bring about the most harm to society.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Having these definitions gives enhanced clarity to online communication services as to what is harmful in Singapore's context.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As a healthcare professional, I am also gratified by the inclusion of content that constitutes a public health risk.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: A 2021 systematic review, which studied the impact of fake news on social media and its influence on health during the COVID-19 pandemic, found that social media platforms have contributed to the infodemic, which can perpetuate fake news and information.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This, in turn, has caused distrust in governments, researchers and health professionals, which directly impacts people's lives and health.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, I have queries on certain aspects of it.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Certain content may be more harmful and may need to be disabled immediately to mitigate the damage.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: One case in point is the Christchurch Attack in 2019.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As Washington Post reporter Drew Harwell summed up in a tweet, "The New Zealand massacre was livestreamed on Facebook, announced on 8chan, reposted on YouTube, commented about on Reddit and mirrored around the world before the tech companies could even react." Secondly, if the OCS fails to comply with IMDA's direction to disable access or is unable to do it within a specified time, under section 45I, Internet service providers (ISPs) can be directed to block Singapore users' access to the OCS.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister clarify how long the OCS is expected to be blocked in such cases and what factors are used to determine the length of time?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, I would also like to seek some clarity on who would be designated a regulated online communication (ROC) provider.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Although section 45K(1) sets out some criteria, they are factors that do not bind IMDA and are actually quite wide.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, how will IMDA quantify or measure "the extent and nature of the effect that different types of OCS have on the people of Singapore"?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Fourthly, section 45L sets out the boundaries of IMDA's powers in the code of practice.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is not clear how IMDA intends to implement the different objectives under section 45L.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Could I seek clarification regarding the type of measures that may be introduced by IMDA under the code of practice?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, how does IMDA intend to have OCS prevent children of different age groups access content that presents a material risk of significant harm to them?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Most already have terms and conditions that require users to declare they are above a certain age.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: If a child user declares falsely, will OCS be liable for the child’s actions?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: If an OCS sets out community terms that explicitly prohibit egregious content but a user posts such content, will OCS be liable for the publishing of such content?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: What safeguards are there to ensure the audits requested by IMDA are not excessive?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: During the time the UK started drafting the online bill, TikTok emerged.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: How often will the code of practice be updated to keep up with these changes?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The constant exposure to disturbing and inappropriate content takes a toll on their well-being.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In 2019, Cambridge Consultants reported that "moderating harmful content can cause significant psychological damage to moderators.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The psychological effects of viewing harmful content is well documented, with reports of moderators experiencing post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms and other mental health issues as a result of the disturbing content that they are exposed to." May I suggest, therefore, that we also make it a part of the code of practice to protect our protectors – the content moderators who risk personal wellness for social good?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to continually improving artificial intelligence (AI), OCS can protect content moderators' mental health through a variety of practices, such as having access to mental health services and support, as well as having exposure limits.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Overall, I am glad that in the drafting of this Bill, extensive industry and public consultations were carried out.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, tackling harmful online content requires a whole-of-society effort.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As the good Minister stated yesterday, laws are not a silver bullet.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is also insufficient and inappropriate to pass the onus of regulating such content on OCS alone without recognising that OCS services are merely a tool or platform that reflects the way individuals use them.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, individuals – parents, children, teachers – law enforcement authorities and governments all have a role to play, too.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone has a part to play by not engaging in online harm, by proactively taking steps to prevent exposure and by supporting those who have become victims of it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, social media platforms are not merely a conduit through which people interact with one another, but they serve as an extension of an individual's being, a representation of who they are and what they stand for.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given how much our digital spaces shape our physical realities, the formation of online communities and groups mirrors the physical society we live in and, therefore, the actions we take and the information we read online bear no less significance than those we do in person and in print.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Behind the personalised content that we see on our social media accounts, there exist complex algorithms with various inputs and metrics that determine what is recommended to us.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With online platforms expected to provide greater clarity regarding how they intend to protect local users from harmful content, users are not only granted the opportunity to make informed decisions but are also able to better understand the decision-making process with regard to appeals and requests they make surrounding egregious content.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To successfully build a safe online environment, it is imperative that users are well-educated on what constitutes harmful conduct and content, and it is my hope that the new measures fulfil this need.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, providing easy and open communication channels will best allow users to voice their concerns as users play an equal part in fostering a safe online environment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While these developments are, indeed, a first step in the right direction, it is important that we do not just stop at this juncture.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While the amendment primarily focuses on specific egregious content that includes posts advocating suicide, self-harm, terrorism, sexual exploitation and other material that risk damaging our social fabric, these are not the only issues that constitute online harm.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we recognise that our online society is very much an extension of the physical society we share in, then we, as a country, should strive to regulate our social media just as we would our physical reality.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is especially important for native issues that arise specifically from the use of social media.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Specifically, in the realm of their public and private posts, and their platform's direct messaging services on issues, such as cyberbullying, doxxing, or even revenge porn.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For a victim to have no agency over information about their private lives being shared online, such an experience can be extremely destabilising and traumatising and, in certain cases, this could even place them at risk of physical harm.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am reminded of a rather vexing and traumatic personal story shared with me by a young lady who was scared, traumatised, worried and confused.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a victim of doxxing, she had her personal details – her name, school, employer, amongst other things – revealed online against her desire by an anonymous account.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When she attempted to remove the post and sought recourse from the social media platform, the lack of urgency in dealing with the matter exacerbated the already extreme levels of vulnerability and fear she experienced, knowing that every extra second the post was allowed to remain online was another opportunity for a vile user to re-victimise her.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even though she had also lodged a Police report, there was no certainty that the report would expedite the removal of her personal identifiable information that has been shared online.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On my part, I had reported the offending account to the social media platform on the same day that the young lady had reached out to me for help.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Because of the high volume of reports we receive, our team hasn’t been able to review this account.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Bullying and harassment are not okay and are against our community guidelines.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are a few things you can do to avoid seeing accounts you find upsetting.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If you don’t want to see xxx on our media platform, you can unfollow, mute, or block them to hide their posts and comments from your feed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If you think this account has posted specific content that shows bullying or harassment, please let us know by reporting the relevant post, comment or story, so we can review it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Clearly, social media platforms ought to take more responsibility in such a situation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With greater clarity, users are better informed and well-assured about how social media platforms can support them upon experiencing online harm.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill is very timely and I appreciate MCI taking proactive steps to put safeguards in place to protect Singaporeans from harmful content, especially those created and distributed with malicious intentions to disrespect, bully, cause division in society, degrade the dignity of persons and of humanity.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In her speech yesterday, the Minister had given many examples of such harms and I trust that we do not need to be persuaded further that it is urgent and imperative for the amendment Bill to pass.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: After listening to hon Member Tin Pei Ling's horror stories involving an avatar in Web 3.0, I am more convinced than ever that we need to take courage to act urgently to protect ourselves, our children and our children's children.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I support the approach which will be taken under the amended Act, but I do have a few questions for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Second, it is good that education of students in schools and Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), as well as education of the general public, will be undertaken in conjunction with the legislation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Education will increase awareness in the vulnerable community and the general public of the prevalence of harmful contents that are lurking in the web and how they can participate in reporting sites or services that carry those contents and, in doing so, be part of the "neighbourhood police" to detect and help to catch bad actors on our Internet and social media platforms.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Just as in the fight against scams, awareness and alertness in the community can go a long way to fight the proliferation of harmful malicious content.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How can volunteers and civic-minded tech-savvy Singaporeans and residents support the Government in this effort?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Third, it is critical that the Government is able to act quickly when there is non-compliance to the Act so that the harmful content does not spread and cause any social epidemic or even pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Like COVID-19, we needed a circuit breaker to ensure that the common good of our society and the social health of our citizens and people are protected.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Whether the content is harmful or otherwise, it may be said to depend on the values of the adult individuals.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How does the Government intend to facilitate the voices of the society to be heard as far as determining what is harmful without compromising the need for swift action to take down the bad actors?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will MCI leverage technology in this war against online harmful content?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Harmful malicious content spreads like virus and we need the Government and the whole of society to fight against this virus of harmful online content together.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill, which is being debated today, is downstream, when the content is already out there, and actions laid out in the Bill are needed to stop the spread and protect Singaporeans from being harmed.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As parents, educators, Government and professionals in the business of communication, we need to focus on moving upstream and pay attention to the need to assist people, especially young people, to develop sound and critical sensing, and to learn how to distinguish truth from falsehood, right from wrong, good from evil.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As a country, it is on us that the soul of our nation and the values of our society are not put at risk, even as I appeal to the conscience of creators of content and online service providers everywhere to do no evil.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, the Government cannot, by itself, ensure online safety for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Internet companies, experts, parents and young people are all essential partners it must work with.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The discussion on online safety also comes at a time when I am being pressured by my daughter, Ella, to allow her to play Roblox.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Actually, she has been nagging me for years to be allowed to play this game, but it has intensified lately as all her friends are playing this game.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am terrified of her being exposed to harmful and inappropriate content online.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope this discussion and this Bill will make steps forward to ensuring a safer online space for our children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification is about the definitions of "egregious content" and "harmful content".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, IMDA's draft of the Code of Practice for Online Safety lists six categories of harmful content.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Social media platforms must "minimise users' exposure" to such content.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the final version of the Code, will IMDA provide more specific category names, detailed explanations for each category or sub-categories for exclusion?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The ambiguity makes it possible for educational or otherwise beneficial content to be caught in the dragnet for harmful content.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, will IMDA also consider adding new categories for harmful content?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, harmful content should include content that promotes extreme beauty standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such content harms our youths by giving them unrealistic expectations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It affects their self-esteem and encourages them to engage in unhealthy behaviour to meet these standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second set of clarifications relates to the scope of these new provisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It seems clear that these regulations will apply to platforms like Facebook, YouTube or TikTok.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But many other companies also use user-generated content.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, e-commerce platforms may rely on user reviews and comments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Online games, as I shared earlier, may have extensive user interaction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if social media services also include online platforms whose core business is not social media?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Private or domestic communications are also excluded from these provisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if this excludes direct messages (DMs) or other user-to-user interactions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a potential channel for harmful content to be transmitted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, a study has found that one in 15 DMs sent by strangers to high-profile women are potentially abusive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify if semi-private communities, such as Discord servers or Telegram groups, will be treated as private or domestic communication?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My last set of clarifications relate to whether we can do more to help individual victims of harmful content.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Victims of revenge porn, cyberbullying or doxxing suffer direct harm to their lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Survivors suffer a loss of dignity and privacy and experience an uphill battle in containing the spread of content once uploaded onto the Internet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three suggestions on how we can help these victims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, funds from penalties under this Bill can be set aside to support these victim-survivors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These funds should be used in partnership with civil society groups who are already active in the community in helping these victims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Platforms could be negligent if they are too slow in taking down harmful content or failing to meet standards in the Code of Practice for Online Safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This duty of care allows the victim to be compensated for their harm under the law of negligence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This duty of care should apply not only to large social media platforms, but all online communication providers, as the potential harm does not discriminate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Small platforms may also be a way to escape detection by sharing harmful content there, then using links to circumvent the safeguards in larger platforms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Individuals who are affected have to rely on themselves to work with the online platform to get the content removed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Going to the Police may not be useful as the Police may lack the jurisdiction or capability to investigate matters of this nature.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that this is a move in the right direction in making the Internet safer for all to use.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I am comforted that measures are now being taken to combat the proliferation of violent and harmful materials online.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Through this Bill, we are sending a strong statement that, in Singapore, we will regulate our online communication services and hold them to a high standard of conduct because there is no place for the public sharing of content that can reasonably be deemed to have a harmful outcome or intent.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Social Media Services (SMS) are listed as a type of OCS.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: With respect to safeguarding children from online harms, rather than tackling this issue primarily from the legislature, robust and comprehensive education programmes should be in place to complement these policies.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I am particularly heartened to see that MOE's Character and Citizenship Education syllabus includes "cyber wellness".

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As part of the syllabus, students learn about navigating cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Students gain knowledge and skills to, one, harness the power of information and communication technology (ICT) for positive purposes; two, maintain a positive presence online; and three, be safe and responsible users of ICT.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Going a step further, I would suggest creating easily accessible safe counselling spaces in schools or create online chatrooms for children to access counselling services if they are adversely affected after an incident or exposure.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Ideally, parents should be the first port of call to address any feelings of confusion, disgust or anxiety that can follow exposure to online harassment.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The reality is that not all parents are equipped or prepared to have such conversations in a helpful, supportive or productive manner.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Children, and even adults, can be severely traumatised by explicit content and hateful language.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: When trauma is left unaddressed and repressed, it can manifest itself in unhealthy ways.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In the code proposed for designated SMS, I would like to propose that tools that allow children and parents to manage online safety and directions to where to seek help if exposed to harmful or inappropriate material be made available.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Toxic behaviours, coarse language, harassment, threats and explicit sexual and violent content are examples of harmful content found in online games.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And while this Bill is not intended to address gaming, perhaps the Ministry can engage the e-sports and gaming community and consider similar protections for players and gamers in the future.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Today, the industry is already recognising toxicity as a problem and some major gaming companies have taken initiatives to launch their own anti-toxicity programmes, but with little success.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As technology and graphics become increasingly sophisticated, many of the most popular games are thrilling and exciting in part because they showcase violent behaviour and explicit conduct with realistic detail.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Storylines and game themes can also depict disagreeable messages and social behaviours.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: With Big Tech firms investing heavily in the metaverse, we can expect more pervasive, more immersive technology and experiences very soon in our everyday lives.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Clearly stated age ratings, warnings and age restrictions are already in place.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Can we better protect children from exposure to sexualisation and violence?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Online gaming may also expose vulnerable groups to Loot Boxes and Gochas.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They are a commonplace in game design and architecture.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They create an element of chance and reward which, in turn, creates a stickiness to the game.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This element of chance may seed undesirable habits which not only affect the players, but their families and persons around them, much like how problem gambling affects a community and not just the gambler alone.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to declare that I am an officer at the Global Esports Federation.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And I would like to say that not all games are violent or gratuitous.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, we should speak openly about gaming and how to game responsibly.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In closing, Mr Deputy Speaker, notwithstanding my clarifications, I am in support of the Online Safety Bill.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The Internet was created to be a tool of empowerment and should be a safe space for Singaporeans to explore and engage freely and securely.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In my speech today, I will touch on how we need to protect our most vulnerable groups and suggest ways that we can further enhance protection, particularly for children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And we all know that content that is racially offensive, that promotes violence against individuals or certain groups and those that try to cause divisions among racial and religious groups, can have a destabilising effect on our society.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In her opening speech, the Minister also mentioned various engagement sessions that showed the growing public concerns amongst Singaporeans with regard to online safety.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, many, if not all, OCS providers have a robust algorithm that removes copyrighted content almost instantaneously.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The technology to remove content automatically and fast already exists and I hope that the social media sites can channel this technology beyond policing copyrighted content and focus also on what is deemed as socially harmful content.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, just as an OCS provider can use technology to aid enforcement, consumers can use technology, too, to circumvent blocked content.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I note that the current draft Code of Practice for Online Safety for Designated Social Media Services does not specify a timeline for compliance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I understand that in some of the European countries, the OCS provider is required to comply with a take-down notice within a stipulated time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am, therefore, curious to know what are the reasons behind the omission of a timeline to comply with the IMDA directive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The speed at which a video of the 2019 New Zealand mosque shooting spread across social media platforms has demonstrated yet again that tech companies are still struggling to control content, especially from popular social media services that offer livestreaming of events.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I read that, in Germany, social media companies, such as Facebook, Twitter, Google and YouTube, are part of a self-regulatory task force committed to removing harmful content quickly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These companies have introduced or improved internal reporting mechanisms and employed local experts to undertake supervision of content.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Will the Ministry consider working with the key OCS providers to establish such a task force in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Children today have grown up with the Internet, and online media is a key part of their daily lives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to various research, social media and other online media have a direct impact on our children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The content that our children see online shapes the way they think and influences how they perceive themselves and others.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Despite many social media services having minimum age limits for new account sign-ups, many young children do have a social media account.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One for their parents to see, and another for their friends which, typically, includes content deemed not suitable for the parents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Against such a backdrop, we must strive to protect our children when they are at an impressionable age and ensure that they have a safe space when they access the Internet and use social media services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For our vulnerable young children, I hope that companies can put in place speed humps to slow down their use of the social media services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While I note that the draft code of practice proposes that the services must minimise users' exposure to harmful content through measures, such as through content moderation measures, these are imperfect and many seemingly innocuous posts can end up being harmful to the very young.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, we should introduce mandatory screen times for very young children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Excessive screen time has been linked to poor development outcomes and we must ensure that our very young do not get hooked onto the never-ending spiral of scrolling mindlessly through social media content.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to statistics from MOE, the number of bullying incidents reported each year to schools has remained low, at about two incidents per 1,000 Primary school pupils and five incidents per 1,000 Secondary school pupils.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I wonder if these figures included online bullying.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In August 2022, a video emerged on social media showing three teenage girls beating up another girl in a carpark.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For every such incident that goes viral, how many more fly undetected under the radar?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What about more subtle, but no less harmful, forms of online bullying, such as posting hateful and "troll" comments among peers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Bullying, including online bullying, impacts the mental health of our children and we need to do all we can to tackle this.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Ministry can review the proposed code of practice and allow users to flag comments or posts that can be deemed as bullying behaviour, so that such harmful content can be addressed promptly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond social media sites, online bullying behaviour is prevalent in online games, too.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As advisor to the Singapore Cybersports and Online Gaming Association, this is an area that I am greatly concerned about, as our children tend to treat what happens in online games very seriously.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In fact, a quick online search will surface many stories about how violence towards women is encouraged amongst gamers who hide under the cover of anonymity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It was later reported that his account was cancelled, but no legal action was taken against him.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The longer we spend on the site, the more advertisements they can serve and the more revenue they can generate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Children, unlike adults, cannot make this trade-off conscientiously and they do not understand the potential unknown side effects from being hooked onto these social media sites.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must, therefore, strive to protect them and introduce speed humps to manage their consumption of such online content.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must also do all we can to stop and prevent online bullying, which can cause real and sometimes deadly, real-world consequences.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If you take into account users who access online social media platforms using their mobile device, the Internet penetration rate goes up higher from 89.5% to around 90%.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The age of such users is also getting younger and younger.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When speaking to children and their parents at community events, I have found that it is no longer surprising for Primary school children to have their own accounts on at least one or two social media platforms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Bill, therefore, is timely in putting in some minimum protections from the increasingly widespread use of online platforms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have some clarifications to seek on the Bill, as well as several comments on how we can make the online aspect of our society a safe and secure place for Singaporeans and Singapore residents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In connection with limb (b), I have two questions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I recall that when the Ukraine conflict broke out in February this year, there were people ringing up the Ukrainian Embassy in Singapore wanting to join the fight in Ukraine.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: MHA even had to put out a statement to warn that it would be an offence to join a foreign war.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, why do we stop at violence, cruelty, abuse or torture on human beings?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are videos of animal cruelty or abuse not equally offensive?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps this can be prescribed as "egregious content", too, under other Part 10A regulations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would also like to seek clarifications on whether there are any other categories of "egregious content" that the Ministry or IMDA is intending to prescribe under regulations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will we also look to censor content which explicitly promotes lifestyles which are not in line with what is presently accepted as norms?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Or the commercialisation of obscene and nude photos and videos?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Should we also designate obvious scam advertisements as "egregious content"?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I look forward to the Minister's response on this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The amendments in this Bill will allow for more effective enforcement against "egregious content", by placing the onus on the online platform providers to disable or block access.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On social media platforms with millions, if not billions, of users, it is more efficient to regulate the platform rather than individual uploaders.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill provides that an electronic service provider is covered so long as it allows content to be accessed in Singapore, unless it is an "excluded electronic service".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would extend to a service that is provided from outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What will stop these foreign service providers from keeping their operations strictly outside Singapore, while flagrantly delivering "egregious content" into Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It appears from the new section 45R(3) that there will be individuals tasked to monitor and flag "egregious content" for the purpose of enforcing these new laws.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would a new department be set up under IMDA or the Singapore Police Force to do this?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What would be the size of this enforcement department?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is relevant because the effectiveness of protection will depend on the speed at which we are able to block and "take down" offensive content.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, back in March 2019 – I believe this example has been shared in many speeches before me – the far-right extremist livestreamed himself on Facebook Live shooting and killing 50 people in the New Zealand mosques.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Facebook, YouTube and Twitter had to fight to take down more than one million copies of the videos circulating online within the first 24 hours.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sure most will agree that that is an obvious example of "egregious content".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But there may also be other types that are more debatable, especially where Singapore's tolerance level and definition of racially or religiously offensive content may differ from the rest of the world or even from the perspective of the content provider or the service provider globally.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How fast do we expect to act to issue disabling and blocking directions to electronic service providers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Government share some detail about the processes it intends to put in place to arrest any unforeseen scenarios promptly?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even after the electronic service providers are issued the disabling or blocking directions, how long will they be given to comply with the directions given?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From a regulatory standpoint, we could legislate higher frequency instead of an annual basis or more frequent audits on how quickly and effectively these electronic service providers act on the user reports that it receives and the systems and processes it has put in place.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are also going to be enhanced regulation of certain platforms that are designated a "regulated online communication service", having regard to the range of services provided to Singapore end-users and the extent and nature of the effect of such services in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Has the Ministry provisionally identified which platforms will be designated as a "regulated online communication service" and whether the Ministry has already engaged with these platforms?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We had a hackaton in Toa Payoh East CC and I had chatted with some of the youths there.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They did share with me a platform called "Discord" – some of the gamers in this House may know about that.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are these processes already ready to be presented to Parliament for consideration?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If not, when can we expect these processes to be finalised and legislated?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides a robust consultation process leading up to the issuance of an online code of practice, may I also suggest that the Ministry think about a periodic consultation process that can be put in place so that industry feedback can be canvassed on amendments that need to be made to an existing online code of practice.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, I understand that this Bill presently targets "egregious content" which should not be appropriate for consumption regardless of age or maturity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On behalf of concerned parents with young or teenage children like myself, I would like to ask if the Ministry foresees that some of the provisions here may be watered down in future to provide for age-specific classification of objectionable content.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My worry there is that it is simply not as easy to verify one's age in the online world as checking one's EZ-Link card or NRIC at the cinema.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, the algorithms on social media platforms that create "echo chambers" with like-minded individuals, while shunning opposing views, also have the risk of deepening divides in our society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While it is understandable for platforms to push products that are matched to user interests so as to maximise advertising revenues, there should be certain controls on pushing views that are consistent with an individual's echo chambers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The latter will only push people towards extremes and worsen the divisiveness of our society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, there is also an observation that society will become less and less informed as social media platforms deprioritise news and other serious content in favour of entertainment-related content.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially acute, given the success of TikTok in recent years, where user clicks are driven more by less serious content and platforms are adapting their algorithms to stay commercially competitive.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have four precocious young children of my own.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Jocelyn and I, like many parents, sometimes relent and allow tablets and smartphones to be their temporary guardians, a salve for those moments that you just need a quick break from parenting.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, truth be told, our fussing and anxiety over them continue even while they quieten down for their much-enjoyed screen time.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As parents, these thoughts do course through our minds: are they playing games that are too violent?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What questionable videos are they accessing, perhaps involuntarily?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Are they being exposed to the wrong company or the wrong content in their online interactions?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We cannot discount that the Internet and social media have been a great force for good over the last two decades.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They have revolutionised education, transformed the global economy, increased the flow of information and knowledge, and also helped us all to keep in touch with one another.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the Internet is like water – a good servant, but a bad master.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As far back as in 1998, our late founding father, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, had described the Internet as a force for both good and evil; that the Internet is as much a purveyor of truth as it is of outright lies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He further pointed out that though it may take some time, morality and wisdom must find a way to control and tame new technology to preserve the fundamental values of society by which parents bring up their children to be good citizens.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Big tech is now so big and so ubiquitous that we have forgotten to be shocked by its growth and its value.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And big tech needs to be held accountable.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us just start by looking at what is deemed by some as the new epidemic of our times: pornographic content on various platforms.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Up until the early 2000s, pornography in all its forms was somewhat isolated, consigned to corners of red-light districts, back alleys of night markets, confined to the margins by social norms and, to some extent, shame.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, by some estimates, the industry is estimated to be worth more than $100 billion annually.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I also believe it still does not go far enough to curb the risk to children through other content.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The safeguards proposed in this Bill require algorithms to be adjusted to prevent any content "detrimental to the physical or mental well-being of children" and to also include automatic parental tools.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But these, as other members have pointed out, can be easily circumvented.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I do agree that, for some, age verification dwells into the realm of privacy, but I think it is the only sure and needed way for content to become age-sensitive for the end user.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the last two years, we have lived through the crisis of a generation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The pandemic has forced us to make uncomfortable decisions at times.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, yet, for the sake of public health, some small sacrifices have had to be made.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has all turned out to be better.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can now freely debate various issues in this hallowed chamber without restrictions because we, collectively, took a sensible course of action.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the lessons of COVID-19 misinformation must not be forgotten.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How easily, in a crisis, public safety can be compromised through fake news, quack treatments and bogus remedies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we had allowed misinformation to run rampant, thousands more could have died.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From COVID-19 conspiracy theorists to vaccine deniers, we could all be in a vastly different situation today if we did not take a rational, science-based, evidential approach.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some of you might be aware, I for one, was badly affected by a booster shot, enough to put me in hospital with still some lasting after-effects, perhaps for the long term.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, despite being amongst a very small minority unfortunate enough to suffer a severe reaction, I believe my decision to be vaccinated was firmly informed by science and evidence rather than to be hoodwinked by online hocus pocus.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We all saw how it could have been vastly different in other countries; even, locally, we have examples.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The elderly lady, taken violently ill and hospitalised because her circle of friends convinced her through mutually shared online fakery, that deworming drug, Ivermectin, was a miracle drug against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And these are just a small sliver of the massive deluge of misinformation online on COVID-19 that have flooded all countries and could have compromised, not just individual health, but the entire community and the safety of various countries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As such, I do wonder if the Ministry has enough manpower to ensure that such egregious content can be expeditiously removed before further harm can be done.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By the same measure of speed of content viralling, the entire industry itself is evolving dramatically day by day.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the major social media platforms have been engaged for this Bill, one of the players, Twitter, has changed hands just last week.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The new owner, Elon Musk, is a free speech absolutist.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He wants to transform Twitter into a platform that, oxymoronically, is a safe haven for all forms of free speech, including harmful ones.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While I also accept that the Bill will similarly evolve and include more industry players, platforms, as the metaverse expands, I do call on the Government to consider including in the very near future social messaging and private messaging platforms where information can spread like wildfire, especially amongst older audiences, and also gaming platforms and chat platforms like Discord, where cyberbullying and misogyny are becoming rampant.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Regulating the metaverse is more challenging than herding cats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, we must act quickly before they run amok.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They decry the chilling effect on free speech that Bills like these introduced elsewhere and here will have on free speech.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But let us look at some surveys of what users themselves want out of their online experience.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, it does show that a safe environment both in the real world and in the online world, are what we aspire to, and we must do what we can.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from regulations, which are needful, I believe that the Ministry would do well to empower all users – adults, parents and children – to do some self-policing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Online safety requires a whole-of-society effort to be educated on what is proper behaviour online personally and what is safe interactions with others.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just as parents cannot simply hand over responsibility, care and control of their children to others in the physical world, we must be aware of our own rights and responsibilities online and how we educate our children to look out for themselves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We do not as yet have to confront the tragedy of Molly Russell within our own country.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As observers, we can sympathise, we can lament; but I think, as parents, it is an experience that no one of us, no child, no family, should have to go through or endure.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our children, especially, need us to take the right decisions to keep them safe.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And so, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support this Bill and hope that my suggestions can be adopted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Harmful content found online has proliferated with the expansion and pervasiveness of social media services in recent years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Bad or irresponsible actors have exploited the accessibility of the digital world to spread harmful materials.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are now in a world where the nature of harm to minors are vastly different.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There has been a pronounced shift from physical to online dangers, but still leading to real and physical harm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As hon Member Alex Yam shared, the suicide of a teenager in the United Kingdom, Ms Molly Russell, in 2017 is a stark reminder of the harms in the online world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the coroner's inquest, they found that the harmful content Molly encountered on social media had played a contributing role in her suicide.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Coroner Andrew Walker said images of self-harm and suicide she viewed "shouldn't have been available for a child to see".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Her death sent shockwaves across the UK and beyond, and the UK is now similarly considering a Bill to the one we are debating today.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: According to Molly's father, Ian Russell, at the inquest, "It's a world I don't recognise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It's a ghetto of the online world that once you fall into it, the algorithm means you can't escape it and it keeps recommending more content.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: You can't escape it." The law must be strengthened so that our minors do not fall into this commercially-driven quicksand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Social media services must take up more responsibility to protect people of all ages, especially minors, from harmful content.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It provides for a calibrated regulatory approach by implementing a code of practice prescribed which social media services must comply or face consequences, along with the authorities' overriding oversight to deal with egregious content.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are just one of the few jurisdictions in the world to consider codifying the responsibilities of these social media services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that many other jurisdictions will follow in time to come.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, we need to refine section A of the code to implement a robust age verification system to effectively delineate a higher standard of responsibility social media services owe to minors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill and the code rightfully prescribe additional obligations to be undertaken by these services to prevent minors from accessing harmful content.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In practical terms, minors would be flagged out as minors by these services if the user inputs their age to show that they are under the age of 18.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With this, the services can then moderate the content shown to minors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: My concern with this is that the current age verification process is very much circumventable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, what if a 12-year-old could falsely input their age as a 21-year-old?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Hence, they would not be treated as a minor as far as the services are concerned.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In such an instance, it must also be the responsibility of the services to implement a secure age verification system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the standards required of the services for such verification?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, would the Ministry also look into implementing a robust nationwide age verification system to ensure that the responsibility of services to children can be adequately effected in practice?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Such nationwide age verification systems are currently being trialed in Australia.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps, this is something that we can also learn from.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, section B of the Code of Practice states that there must be an easy-to-use mechanism for Singapore end-users to report harmful content and unwanted interaction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, clauses which directly relate to the liability of the services arising from their failure to comply with user requests in the code are not readily apparent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Ministry establish an avenue for Singapore end-users to report such non-compliance with the code?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Further, I understand that even though the code is still under review, section B, which imposes obligations on the services to act on user reports in a timely manner, seems to leave some room for ambiguity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry elaborate on whether it would consider implementing an objective or specific timeframe for the services to respond to user reports and perhaps have different timeframes which are proportionate to the nature of the harmful content identified?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the timeframe for services to respond to sexual cyberbullying content should arguably be done as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that online safety is as equally important as privacy and data protection, if not even more.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Both are crucial gears that must be safeguarded in the digital ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This would also give the Ministry more flexibility in proposing appropriate penalties based on the non-compliance complained of.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On a related note, the current penalties almost seem like a slap on the wrist, compared to other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This remains a key piece in this journey.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.07 pm until 3.30 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: All 16 Members who spoke have given their support, reflecting the broad consensus on the need and timeliness of the proposals.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members raised many useful points which I will address.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked what other types of services, besides social media services, may be specified in the Schedule of Online Communication Services, or OCS.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Dr Shahira Abdullah wanted to know how IMDA will decide which service providers to designate.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: She and Ms Tin Pei Ling also asked about updating our regulations to keep in step with new technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: IMDA will use various data sources on user trends in Singapore to aid these assessments.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Government is actively studying several areas, but I seek Members’ understanding that it can be counter-productive to discuss them prematurely.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Let us instead better understand and characterise the issues, taking reference from regulatory attempts elsewhere, before moving to design a suitable set of interventions for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Alex Yam, Mr Gerald Giam and Mr Mark Chay asked about online gaming, whereas the Bill only covers social media services currently.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have been thinking about it and we will share more details when ready.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: IMDA will consult services before designating them under the Bill, to ensure that designated services are clear on the requirements and are given the opportunity to provide input on the proposals laid out by IMDA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Leon Perera asked about the consultation process.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Details will be set out on how IMDA will work closely with the designated services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Having built constructive relationships with many of these services over the years, we are confident the processes will be robust.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The list of services to be designated eventually will be published by IMDA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms Nadia Samdin, Mr Alex Yam and Ms Tin Pei Ling asked why private communications have been excluded.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The short answer is that there are legitimate privacy concerns, which Mr Gerald Giam also shares.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: IMDA’s draft Code of Practice for Online Safety will require designated social media services to provide easily accessible user reporting mechanisms throughout its service.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If individuals encounter harmful messages or unwanted interactions in private messages when using these social media services, they could block the sender or report the sender to the service.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In such instances, IMDA will be empowered to take the same actions against them.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Zhulkarnain asked about the specific factors in determining whether communications are private, that could shield such services from complying with IMDA’s protective measures.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Labelling a group or communications as private does not make it so.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill sets out a list of factors that must be considered collectively.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, it may be possible to conclude that a social media group is public, even if that social media group has been set to “private” and requires the owner to grant permission before one can access the content, but the owner is indiscriminate in granting that access.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to study this issue closely with other agencies, industry and international partners.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Next, on what type of content the Bill will, or will not, address.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked whether drug abuse and other illegal activities will be covered.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Saktiandi highlighted a particular area in the online domain that is of growing concern to many users – scams.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under “egregious content”, as defined under the Bill, content that may cause risk to public health will be covered.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Depending on the facts of the case, this may include drug-related content.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: IMDA’s Code of Practice for Online Safety also requires services to apply content moderation systems to vice and organised crime, including fraud and scam content.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Gerald Giam and Mr Leon Perera asked whether the Bill would cover non-consensual sharing of intimate images, and Mr Louis Ng asked why content “likely to cause feelings of enmity, hatred, ill will or hostility” is applied only to racial and religious groups, and not to other demographic segments, such as gender.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To a large extent, the kinds of problematic content the Members have in mind will already be covered within the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Content that advocates or instructs on violence, including sexual violence, to individuals will be covered.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: IMDA’s draft code of practice for Online Safety will require services to assess and act on cyberbullying, including content that is likely to cause harassment, alarm or distress to the user, which Mr Leon Perera and Mr Darryl David, as well as Mr Melvin Yong, also emphasised the need for.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For cases of harassment, there may also be recourse under laws, such as the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To Mr Louis Ng’s question on providing more details of “harmful content” under the Code, IMDA has issued a set of draft guidelines giving examples of the content covered, which will be finalised together with the Code.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Leon Perera spoke at length about the problem of loot boxes in online gaming.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This matter falls under the Gambling Control Act, but since Members have raised it, I will briefly address it.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I invite the Members to file Parliamentary Questions if they wish to discuss this issue in greater detail.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Saktiandi also raised queries on content, such as lifestyles that go against traditional norms of society, participation in foreign armed conflicts, animal cruelty and commercialised nudity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Should we go beyond concerns over safety of individuals and communities to cover other types of content at this juncture?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This has the same problem as if our proposals attempted to cover other types of services prematurely.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill will become unwieldy, our proposals lacking in focus and the results likely ineffective.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin asked if we had considered streamlining all online-related harms into the Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our approach has been to identify and address specific areas of harm in a targeted manner.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As to whether the laws will be consolidated later, that remains to be seen.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At this time, it is more important that we put in place legislation that effectively addresses and combats the respective harms.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, at the Committee of Supply debates this year, MHA announced that it was studying potential levers to deal with criminal offences committed online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These levers are envisioned to complement the provisions under the Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
